name: Asunción Mixtepec Zapotec
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.source_named: Nearly extinct Zapotec variety; Glottolog lists no grammar/phonology and no documentation beyond survey mentions was located.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian & Ryan Bennett. 2020 [2018 preprint]. Prosody in Mesoamerican languages (held by the project:).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Cites Sicoli 2007 only for Lachixío Zapotec among languages with 'alternating, head-initial trochaic stress'; no entry for Asunción Mixtepec.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en): 'Asunción Mixtepec Zapotec' and 'Zapotec languages' (wikitext saved).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Stub: 'North Central Zimatlan Zapotec', nearly extinct, '22% intelligible with Ayoquesco' (Ethnologue); Merrill 2008 regional list leaves Asunción Mixtepec unplaced ('apparently divergent'). Generic Zapotec statement (stress on the penultimate syllable of the root where described) is not language-specific.

sources.citation: Sicoli, Mark A. 2021. Deliberate decisions and unintended consequences: Ratifying nonspeakers through code alternation in child-directed speech. In Anna M. Babel & Mark A. Sicoli (eds.), Contact, Structure, and Change: A Festschrift in Honor of Sarah G. Thomason, 3-31. Ann Arbor: Maize Books. (whole OA volume. also ch. 11, Eric W. Campbell, On Zapotecan glottal stop, and where (not) to reconstruct it)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress for [zoo]. p.3-4 confirms Asunción Mixtepec was in Sicoli's PhD field region ('the small frontier town of Asunción Mixtepec where Zapotec was already moribund during my PhD work (subsequently published as Sicoli 2011)'); p.5-6 lists the West Zapotec towns he surveyed (the Mixtepecs listed there are San Miguel, San Mateo, Santa Cruz -- not Asunción). Campbell's ch. 11 has no Asunción Mixtepec data.

sources.citation: Bueno Holle, Juan José. 2019. Information structure in Isthmus Zapotec narrative and conversation (Topics at the Grammar-Discourse Interface 3 / LangSci 219). Berlin: Language Science Press. sec. 2.2.2 (read from OAPEN text, not copied to the asun1236 folder).
sources.note: Second-hand summary of Sicoli 2007's prosody chapters, explicitly about Lachixío Zapotec: 'only primary (no secondary) stress which is non-iterative', maximal phonological word [[proclitic [stressed root]] enclitic], 'The metrical foot.. is trochaic'. Nothing about Asunción Mixtepec.

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2018. La inteligibilidad y la autodenominación en la clasificación de lenguas zapotecas de la Sierra Sur y más allá (INALI coloquio slides); Beam de Azcona 2018. Diversificación y convergencia: una reconsideración del 'zapoteco de la Sierra Sur' (UNISON talk).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Southern Zapotec classification only; repeats the Zapotec root-initial vs Chatino root-final stress generalization; Asunción Mixtepec absent.

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2016. Zapotecan languages. Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics (author postprint, 26 pp.).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Family-level only: 'A stress shift from the final syllable (retained in Chatino) to the first (usually penultimate) syllable of the root (in Zapotec)' (summary p.1) and 'a shift from traditional Otomanguean final stress to stem-initial stress in Zapotec (Kaufman, 1993-2014; Campbell, 2013a)' (p.4). Asunción Mixtepec not mentioned.

sources.citation: Sicoli, Mark A. 2010. Shifting voices with participant roles: Voice qualities and speech registers in Mesoamerica. Language in Society 39(4): 521-553.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lachixío Zapotec [zpl] voice registers, low tone as imperative marker, low-tone > breathy phonotactics; no word-stress statement; Asunción Mixtepec not mentioned.

sources.citation: INALI. 2008. Catálogo de las lenguas indígenas nacionales, agrupación zapoteco (web edition).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress; identity only: Asunción Mixtepec (mun. San Bernardo Mixtepec) is listed under the variant <zapoteco de Valles, oeste> (dixasà / dizë) with Magdalena Mixtepec, San Bernardo Mixtepec, San Pablo Cuatro Venados and San Pablo Huixtepec.

sources.citation: Sicoli, Mark. 2000 [BLS 25, 1999]. Loanwords and contact-induced phonological change in Lachixío Zapotec. Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 25: 395-406. doi 10.3765/bls.v25i1.1194 (scan; scanned at 300 dpi).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lachixío only ('a dialect of the Solteco branch.. spoken in Sola de Vega and Southwest Zimatlan'): native words are CVTV/TV with the medial obstruent 'after a stressed syllable' (p.398-399); 'final syllable stress' in late Spanish loans such as kolchón 'violate[s] the system of phonological constraints that were operational in the precontact Lachixío phonological system' (p.396) -- i.e. implicit root-initial/penultimate stress for Lachixío. Nothing on Asunción Mixtepec.

sources.citation: Sicoli, Mark A. 2020. Saying and Doing in Zapotec: Multimodality, Resonance, and the Language of Joint Actions. London: Bloomsbury (doi 10.5040/9781350142190); Spanish OA translation 'Decir y hacer en zapoteco', UVA LibraOpen 9p290951g.

sources.citation: Sicoli, Mark A. 2011. Agency and ideology in language shift and language maintenance. In Tania Granadillo & Heidi A. Orcutt-Gachiri (eds.), Ethnographic Contributions to the Study of Endangered Languages, 161-176. Tucson: University of Arizona Press.

sources.citation: Kaufman, Terrence, Mark Sicoli et al. 2007-2010. Survey of Zapotec and Chatino languages (INALI/PDLMA phonological-lexical questionnaires; audio and transcriptions archived at AILLA, University of Texas).

sources.note: If Asunción Mixtepec was among the ~100 towns surveyed, this is the only primary phonetic record (transcribed wordlists with tone/stress marking) of the variety; AILLA was bot-blocked (Anubis) by automated download so inclusion could not be verified.
